articles.title: In 2025, Mowi launched Chileâs first floating solar salmon farm; now it supplies 57% of its power and saving 36,750 gallons of diesel a year
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For years, diesel has been a practical part of running salmon farms in remote coastal waters, where connecting to a conventional electricity grid is o.
articles.body: For years, diesel has been a practical part of running salmon farms in remote coastal waters, where connecting to a conventional electricity grid is often difficult. That is beginning to change at one of Mowiâs sites in southern Chile. In June 2025, the company introduced what it described as Chileâs first floating solar cage at its Isla Huar salmon farm in the Los Lagos region. The installation combines solar panels fitted to the farming structure with batteries that can store electricity for use when sunlight is unavailable. A year on, the project is reported to be supplying about 57% of the siteâs power requirements. It is also expected to save around 139,200 litres of diesel each year, equivalent to roughly 36,750 US gallons. The figures offer an early indication of what renewable power can do for an offshore salmon farm operating far from the grid.Why Mowiâs 2025 floating solar cage in Chile mattersMowi announced the project in June 2025, describing it as Chileâs first floating solar cage. The installation was developed with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime at the companyâs Isla Huar operation. Rather than placing solar panels on land, the system puts them directly on the floating farming infrastructure, where they have to cope with wind, waves and the demands of an offshore working environment.According to the official Mowi site, the hybrid arrangement was designed to reduce fuel use and cut emissions. The company estimated an annual reduction of 350 tonnes of COâ. Its announcement also explained how the electricity would be handled: power from the floating solar plant could either be used immediately or stored in batteries for later use. The system was initially expected to cover up to half of the centreâs energy requirements.How battery storage keeps Mowiâs floating solar salmon farm runningThe panels are only part of the system. Battery storage is what allows electricity generated during periods of sunshine to remain available when solar production falls. Alotta, which supplied the floating solar technology, describes the installation as a hybrid system designed to provide power continuously rather than simply producing electricity when the sun is shining.In its account of the Chilean project, Alotta said the system covers approximately 50% of the siteâs energy requirements and combines solar generation with integrated battery storage. The company also operates the project under an energy-as-a-service model, meaning Mowi purchases renewable electricity rather than having to operate the entire energy installation itself. Alotta described the arrangement as a way of making the technology easier to use at remote aquaculture sites.Why cutting diesel use matters for Mowiâs remote salmon farmThe newer figures from AKVA group put the renewable contribution at around 57% of the farmâs energy needs. The company says the system is expected to reduce annual diesel consumption by approximately 139,200 litres. That is roughly 36,750 US gallons of fuel that would no longer need to be burned each year. The same reduction is associated with about 350 tonnes of COâ emissions annually.That reduction matters at a farm that operates away from a conventional electricity grid. Diesel is not only used as a fuel source; it also has to be transported to the site. Cutting consumption therefore reduces the amount of fuel that has to be delivered by boat. AKVA says the project is also expected to reduce noise from diesel generators, changing the working conditions around the farm while lowering the amount of boat traffic associated with refuelling.Why Mowiâs floating solar project could become a model for remote salmon farmsThe project is attracting attention because remote aquaculture sites often need reliable electricity but are located far from conventional power grids. Solar panels and battery storage can provide local power, while diesel generators remain available when renewable energy is insufficient. As per Alotta, its floating solar technology was previously tested along the Norwegian coast before being introduced in Chile. Mowi developed the project with AKVA group, Alotta Energy and Fjord Maritime to improve energy efficiency and reduce emissions.For Mowi, the goal is to reduce diesel use rather than eliminate it. The reported 57% renewable contribution means solar power and batteries supply a significant share of the farmâs electricity, with diesel kept as backup. If the projected 139,200-litre annual reduction is achieved, the system could also reduce the amount of fuel that needs to be transported to the remote site.Launched in 2025 as Chileâs first floating solar-powered salmon-farming installation, the project demonstrates how renewable energy and battery storage can be added to existing offshore operations. The technology partners say the system is designed to provide about 57% of the farmâs electricity and cut diesel use by roughly 36,750 gallons a year, potentially offering a model for other remote aquaculture sites.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu shares why giving employees more freedom can feel âchaoticâ; says âThere is always â¦â
articles.summary: Tech News News: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has shared his views on a workplace question many companies face: Should employees wait for instructions from their leaders.
articles.body: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has shared his views on a workplace question many companies face: Should employees wait for instructions from their leaders or take the initiative and act on their own? In a post on X (formerly known as Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said giving people more freedom to take initiative can create an energetic but sometimes chaotic work culture. Employees may disagree strongly with one another and constantly feel that things can be improved. âThere is always the gnawing feeling of ânot good enoughâ,â Vembu wrote, explaining the trade-off between certainty and initiative in an organisation.Sridhar Vembu on why freedom can feel âchaoticâIn the post, Sridhar Vembu said highly metric-driven organisations often create a culture where employees wait for instructions from the top. Such workplaces can offer more predictability and certainty.However, he warned that this approach has its risks. âUnless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost,â Vembu wrote.On the other hand, an organisation where people are encouraged to take initiative can be less predictable. Employees with energy and strong ideas may disagree with each other, he said.âSeize the initiative cultureâ often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements. There is always the gnawing feeling of ânot good enoughâ,â Vembu wrote.Sridhar Vembu: 'Every smart programmerâ thinks they can do betterThe Zoho founder also used programmers as an example to explain why initiative-driven workplaces can see frequent disagreements.âPeople who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other,â he wrote, adding: âI joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks âit sucks, I can do betterâ!âAccording to Vembu, this is the trade-off companies need to understand when building their culture. A workplace can provide employees with comfortable certainty but risk losing their initiative. Alternatively, it can encourage people to take initiative while accepting the discomfort and disagreements that may come with it.Hereâs the post shared by Sridhar Vembu"On org culture: Do people wait for instructions from the top? Or do they seize the initiative and run?Highly metric driven orgs tend to produce the "wait for instructions from the top" culture and there is more predictability and certainty in that culture. Unless the top always knows how to set the right course, the org can be lost."Seize the initiative culture" often feels chaotic, with lots of internal disagreements. There is always the gnawing feeling of "not good enough". In a chaotic initiative-driven culture, the external environment (market) may have to provide the occasional discipline.People who are full of energy and initiative often vehemently disagree with other. I joke about this: every smart programmer looks at another programmer's code and thinks "it sucks, I can do better"!That is your trade-off in org cultures. We can provide comfortable certainty but lose the initiative or we can seize the initiative but keep feeling somewhat uncomfortable.In my experience, trying to square this circle: "we will have a highly disciplined culture of seizing the initiative" produces the worst of both worlds."Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Amazon and Flipkart have new cancellation fees for sellers and why they are unhappy with it
articles.summary: Tech News News: The story has been updated with a statement from Amazon.Online commerce platforms Amazon and Flipkart have restructured cancellation fees ahead of the.
articles.body: The story has been updated with a statement from Amazon.Online commerce platforms Amazon and Flipkart have restructured cancellation fees ahead of the festival season in the country. According to a report by PTI, Amazon India has changed the manner in which it calculates order cancellation fees for sellers using its Easy Ship and Self Ship services. As per the notice on Amazon Indiaâs seller forum, the change is effective from August 17. Similarly, Flipkart has also put in place a three-tier penalty structure for lapses in order fulfilment, effective August 23, 2026. The changes, sellers say, adds to the financial burden on small and medium enterprises already operating on thin margins, the report states.Commenting on the report, an Amazon spokesperson said : âCustomer and seller experience is at the heart of everything we do at Amazon. We expect orders placed by customers to be fulfilled reliably by sellers on our marketplace. To encourage timely and dependable fulfilment, we have revised cancellation fees for Easy Ship and Self-Ship sellers. This fee is conditional and only applies in the rare event of a seller-initiated cancellation, which accounts for less than 1% of orders on Amazon.in. We have appropriate measures in place to ensure sellers are protected when cancellations are due to circumstances beyond their control.âWhat is Amazonâs Easy Ship and Self Ship servicesUnder Self Ship, a seller on Amazon packs and delivers the product themselves, using their own courier or delivery service. No Amazon logistics are involved in self ship.As explained in the PTI report, the cancellation fee was earlier based on category-specific referral charges. But after the new change, it will now be computed as a percentage of the order value.âUnder the revised structure, sellers are charged 10% of the order value for orders below Rs 10,000, 8% for orders between Rs 10,001 and Rs 50,000, 5% for orders between Rs 50,001 and Rs 1,00,000, and 2% for orders above Rs 1,00,000, with an 18% goods and services tax levied in addition,â the report says.The cancellation fee is applicable both when a seller cancels an order for reasons other than a buyer's request, and when an order is automatically cancelled because the seller does not ship and confirm the shipment within 24 hours of the estimated ship date.Amazon to increase closing fees across its Fulfillment CenterAmazon is also increasing the closing fees across its Fulfillment Center, Easy Ship, and Seller Flex channels. According to the PTI report, the change will be effective from September 7, 2026.For those unaware, Amazon charges a closing fee every time a product is sold on its platform. The fee depends on the product's price range and the fulfillment channel used by the seller. The fee will increase by Re 1 for products priced up to Rs 500 and by Rs 3 for products priced above Rs 500. Amazon said the increase is due to rising fuel and logistics costs.What is Flipkartâs three-tier penalty structureFlipkart has introduced a three-tier penalty system for sellers who fail to meet order fulfilment deadlines. The new policy came into effect on August 23, 2026. Under the new structure, sellers will be charged Rs 30 per shipment if an order is not ready for pickup by the committed Dispatch By Date (DBD). As stated in the PTI report, a seller cancellation, or an automatic cancellation after three missed dispatch deadlines, will attract a Rs 60 penalty per shipment. If an order is delayed and later cancelled, the penalty will rise to Rs 90 per shipment.Earlier, missing a DBD deadline could lead to a seller's account being temporarily locked, which could have a bigger impact on their business. New sellers will not be covered by the policy for the first three months of their selling journey. People aware of the development told PTI that the new system aims to encourage better planning by sellers and improve the customer experience.What sellers sayAs cited in the PTI report, some sellers said that cancellations were at times caused by factors outside their control, such as delivery personnel failing to arrive for a scheduled pickup. They also questioned why cancellation fees should apply to the seller in such instances.Another seller said the difference in total fees between sellers using Amazon's fulfilment network and those on Easy Ship could be as high as Rs 45 per unit on comparable orders, which the seller claims, creates an unfair competitive situation.The PTI report quotes Vinod Kumar, Trustee of the Forum for Internet Resellers, Sellers and Traders (FIRST INDIA), who said Indian online sellers recognise the need for timely fulfilment and high customer service standards, but that the recent increase in cancellation, dispatch and other seller penalties by major e-commerce marketplaces, particularly ahead of the festive season, was a matter of concern for MSMEs already facing thin margins and rising costs."Sellers should not become the default financial shock absorbers of the e commerce ecosystem. Marketplaces must ensure transparent attribution of responsibility, reasonable and proportionate penalties, adequate advance notice of fee changes and a simple mechanism to challenge wrongful charges. The objective should be to improve fulfilment while making digital commerce more, not less, viable for small businesses," Kumar added.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: OnlyFans owner was paid over $700m before his death
articles.summary: The site hosts a range of subscription-based content from cooking to fitness videos, but it is best known for pornography.
articles.body:
The late owner of streaming platform OnlyFans was paid more than $700m (£513m) in dividends before his death from cancer earlier this year.

Fenix International Ltd, the British company that owns OnlyFans, made $714m in profit before tax last year, it said in its annual report. This is an increase of 5% from 2024.

The site hosts a range of subscription-based content from cooking to fitness videos, but it is best known for pornography and is credited with transforming online adult content by encouraging personal connection between sex workers and subscribers.

Its owner Leonid Radvinsky, who died earlier this year aged 43 , bought the site from its British founders in 2018.

OnlyFans employs just 47 people. Companies with such high profits rarely have such small staff - for example, British retail giant Marks and Spencer, which employs over 65,000 people, made £671m in profit last year.

Fenix International's company results show that it paid dividends of $535m for the year ending 30 November 2025, with further dividends payments totalling $174m between then and 26 March 2026.

Radvinsky, who was born in Ukraine and raised in the US, died on 23 March. The company is now owned by his widow, Yekaterina 'Katie' Chudnovsky.

OnlyFans surged in popularity during the Covid-19 pandemic, landing Radvinsky on Forbes' annual list of billionaires just three years later.

The site is known for the way it encourages creators and fans to connect through livestreams, personalised messages, and direct requests for custom-made photos and videos.

In return for hosting the material, OnlyFans takes a 20% share of all payments.

The site had 132 million paying subscribers and 2.5 million active creators in 2025.

The boom in size and popularity under Radvinsky's ownership also brought scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators over its adult content — a recent BBC Three documentary uncovered allegations of exploitation, coercion and violence committed against OnlyFans creators.

In 2024, British regulators launched an investigation into whether children were accessing porn , an issue that the company at the time blamed on a technical issue.

Ofcom ultimately dropped that probe, but it fined the firm about £1m for failing to respond accurately to its requests for information about the measures it had in place to check the age of its users, who in theory must be 18 or over.

Creators have also debunked the narrative that making explicit videos on the site is a get-rich-quick scheme.

Keily Blair, the chief executive of OnlyFans, said on Tuesday that the company had paid over $30bn to creators since launching a decade ago.

"OnlyFans provides real opportunities to real people by creating a safe, regulated space where people can monetise their content with a global fan base," she said.

"As a UK-based business we have also made a significant contribution to the UK economy, paying over £600 million in corporate taxes from 2016 to date."

articles.title: Mysterious 3,000-year-old hoard with violently smashed sword emerges during construction project
articles.summary: Metal detecting led archaeologists to a Bronze Age hoard of deformed sickles, a shattered sword blade and ingots deposited in a flooded Czech Republic wetland.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Central Europe recently came across an unusual hoard of Bronze Age tools — including a sword that had been deliberately smashed with a powerful blow. The discovery was announced by Archaeological Center Olomouc (ACO), a research institution in the Czech Republic, on August 12. The hoard was found in a heavily flooded area at the end of May. The cache, discovered near Kojetín in central Moravia during archaeological work connected to a railway project, contained an assortment of worn and broken bronze objects. MYSTERY DEEPENS AFTER 2,700-YEAR-OLD BRONZE SWORD EMERGES STANDING UPRIGHT The artifacts included eight deformed sickles, one intact sickle, part of a sword blade, ornament fragments, three ingots and two unfinished objects. "Use-wear analysis has shown that most of the bronze objects had been used before their deposition and that some were deliberately damaged," ACO officials said in a statement. Pictures show the mud-covered Bronze Age artifacts shortly after their discovery.  The sword bore particularly dramatic signs of damage, with archaeologists concluding that it had been struck apart with a single powerful blow. "[It was] probably delivered with a chisel or an axe, while several of the sickles were intentionally deformed," the ACO release read. 1,740-YEAR-OLD ROMAN COIN BEARING EMPEROR'S NAME FOUND AS ENGLAND RAIL DIG REVEALS CLUES Lead archaeologist Vít Záhorák told officials the team's decision to use metal detecting was crucial to finding the objects. "We knew our work was continuing in an area occupied by an extensive prehistoric settlement, so we also used metal-detecting survey during the archaeological monitoring," said Záhorák. "It was this method that led to the discovery of the bronze hoard." "It was this method that led to the discovery of the bronze hoard," he added.  While it may seem plausible that the tools were concealed as a temporary hiding place, officials say the evidence points to a more ceremonial purpose. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "The current interpretation instead suggests that the objects were deliberately deposited in a former wetland and that their deposition may have formed part of a ritual practice," the statement said. Officials noted that the Kojetín discovery has parallels with other Bronze Age sites. "Deposits of bronze objects in watery or waterlogged settings are also known from other Bronze Age sites," the statement read. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "In some of these cases, archaeologists have considered a possible connection with ritual practices. Further specialist analyses will help determine whether the Kojetín hoard had a comparable significance." The artifacts are currently undergoing conservation and analysis by specialists. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The Bronze Age hoard is far from the only archaeological discovery to emerge in the Czech Republic in recent years. Last year, officials announced the discovery of multiple military graves during highway construction, including one dating back to the 1745 Battle of Žďár during the Second Silesian War. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP This spring, ACO officials reported finding over 1,000 ancient artifacts spanning during excavations along a future high-speed railway route.

articles.title: Father's house was rammed by car before son died in A66 crash
articles.summary: The house belonging to Cole Worthy's father is significantly damaged and its windows are smashed.
articles.body:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash , as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

The rammed house is a red bricked semi-detached that sits in a quiet residential street in Acklam.

The downstairs bay window has been smashed, with bricks scattered beneath it, and an upstairs bedroom window has also been broken.

Neighbours, who did not want to be identified, said Worthy sometimes stayed at his father's property.

Locals described hearing loud bangs at around two in the morning on Saturday and said the street had been full of police all weekend.

Meanwhile, nine men and three women, aged between 18 and 61, were arrested across Teesside on Monday as part of the investigation into the lead-up to the crash. They were held on a range of offences, including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

Kai Beattie, of Foxrush Court, Redcar, has been charged with possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

Cameron George, of Micklow Close, Redcar, has been charged with possession of class A and class B drugs with intent to supply, and possession of criminal property.

Cleveland Police said on Tuesday that five further arrests had been made, including a 16-year-old boy and two men, 18 and 21, who were held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group.

A 55-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and a 23-year-old man on suspicion of making threats to kill.

Those previously arrested as part of the investigation are:

Three men, aged 24, 19 and 35, all held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon. They are in police custody.

A man, 21, held on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison

A 30-year-old woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and who is in police custody

A 20-year-old man arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order. He remains in custody

A 26-year-old man was charged with possession with intent to supply class A drugs, as well as the possession of criminal property. He was remanded in custody ahead of his next court hearing

Another man, 39, and a 47-year-old woman have been released on conditional bail after both being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

An 18-year-old man has been released on unconditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs, and possession of class C drugs

A 61-year-old woman has been released on conditional bail after being arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate

A 39-year-old man has been arrested on suspicion of threats to kill and has been released on conditional bail

articles.title: Musk's data centers push out family that's owned land for generations
articles.summary: A plant in Southaven, Mississippi, that powers Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the area has sparked backlash from residents concerned about noise and ai...
articles.body:
On a 2-acre property in Mississippi , 52-year-old Krystal Polk's family lived off the land for generations, raising chickens and pigs, growing onions and herbs and trading their peaches for pears.

The land, on the border with Tennessee in the city of Southaven, was her family's survival, Polk said. "We lived a very simplistic life," she told CBS News.

While life there may have been simple in Polk's view, the circumstances surrounding her home rarely ever were. Her family acquired the property "before people of color were allowed to have land," she said, and it's been passed down for four generations. When Polk's parents first moved in, they discovered "KKK" scrawled at the bottom of the hill of their property, she said.

Holding on to the land was made more difficult a year ago when a noisy neighbor appeared across the street — a power plant so loud, it drove the family away. Since then, the land has sat mostly empty, occupied only by an unrelenting hum.

The plant, which is powering Elon Musk's SpaceXAI data centers in the Memphis area, has sparked backlash from Southaven residents concerned about noise and air pollution. A petition by the resident-run Safe and Sound Coalition calling to shut down the power plant has over 1,400 signatures.

Polk said she remembers when she could hear the birds chirping at her family home. Now, she said the plant's "constant roaring" lingers in her ears even after she leaves.

"It's like you're in the middle of the airport where the planes are taking off, but they never take off," she said.

SpaceXAI, formerly known as xAI, recently said in a July press release that it is investing millions of dollars in sound walls and silencers with "advanced quieting technologies" around the plant. Southaven residents have told CBS News that one sound wall installed so far has provided little reprieve from the noise.

Over the course of two years, Musk has expanded his footprint in the Memphis region starting with the construction of his Colossus 1 data center just north of Southaven in 2024. By January 2026, two more data centers were announced. This July, Musk quietly confirmed the construction of another local data center, "Minihard," in a reply to a post on his platform X.

Musk's SpaceXAI projects will total more than $20 billion in investments to Southaven, which Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves said in a press release will "bring amazing opportunities to its residents for generations."

But for Polk, the development has meant a new kind of strain on her family.

"We don't know the future," she said. "So we're not sure what to invest into it."

Polk moved away from the family home after getting married, and for years, it bounced between relatives. It was where Polk churned her own ice cream as a child, held her rehearsal dinner when she got married and hosted the holidays each year.

"We gathered there and we thanked God for what we had," she said. "It was always a celebration."

She planned to return as a retiree and eventually pass the property down to her children. But now, those plans have been put on hold. Apart from the "24/7" noise, Polk said she and her family have asthma and are concerned about fumes from the gas turbines at the plant.

"I'm afraid that we will be the ones that everyone looks back on and says, 'Hey, remember they tried to tell us that these things were hazardous to our health and causing harm,'" Polk said. "I'm afraid that we're going to be those casualties."

The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and other groups sued xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in April, alleging that the plant "emits significant amounts of harmful pollutants."

In June, SpaceXAI filed a motion to dismiss the case, and the Department of Justice also moved to intervene and dismiss the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that the matter "concerns national security and Mississippi's lawful action regarding permitting" and that the NAACP's lawsuit "could hinder the War Department's use of AI for national defense."

CBS News reached out to SpaceXAI multiple times for comment and has not heard back.

The company has entered into an agreement with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality that includes removing the 69 temporary turbines at the plant and replacing them with 41 permanent turbines over the course of a year.

But a study conducted by EmPower Analytics Group, an independent consulting firm that provides scientific analysis of the health impact of AI infrastructure, found that the plan to install dozens of gas turbines would increase air pollution in the area and would be concentrated in communities that are disproportionately Black.

The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality said in a statement that it doesn't comment on "third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation" and that it "remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations."

MDEQ said that as part of the permitting process, MZX Tech was required to demonstrate that the proposed facility would not violate air quality standards.

Still, residents are not convinced. Shannon Samsa, a 27-year-old physician assistant living in Southaven, is concerned about the plant's impact on her community's health. She's become an outspoken advocate against the plant, speaking up at city meetings and leading the Safe and Sound Coalition as its director.

"It's not just my neighbors, it's not just my family and friends, it's my future patients," she said. "It's also a huge healthcare issue."

As SpaceXAI extends its reach in the region, the future of Polk's property hangs in the balance. Some companies have expressed interest in purchasing it.

Polk said she was approached by real estate firm Cushman & Wakefield with an offer. After multiple "nos" over the course of weeks, she said she eventually filed a Better Business Bureau complaint, accusing the company of harassment and manipulation.

In the complaint, reviewed by CBS News, Polk alleged the firm's Tennessee branch tried to coerce her into agreeing to services.

Cushman & Wakefield, in response to the complaint, said it was exploring the potential acquisition of Polk's land on behalf of a client, who was not identified. The firm confirmed it made multiple attempts to contact Polk "by phone, text and written correspondence," but denied engaging in "harassment, pressure tactics, or inappropriate conduct." CBS News reached out to Cushman & Wakefield and did not receive a response.

Polk said the company has not reached out since she filed the complaint. She declined to disclose Cushman & Wakefield's offer, but said that "it was not worth anything."

Selling the land is complicated — keeping it was her father's dying wish, Polk said.

"He asked me to please keep it as much as I could within reason," she said. "I'm not sure if you could offer a value."

articles.title: 'What women wears is her choice':  Rahul Gandhi backs Kriti Sanon over Raksha Bandhan ad row
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday defended actor Kriti Sanon amid criticism of her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan a.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday defended actor Kriti Sanon amid criticism of her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan advertisement, saying "what women wears is her choice."In a post on Instagram, Gandhi said, "What a woman wears, what she does and where she goes - is her choice." "Stop trolling women for exercising their freedom," he added.Rahul's remarks came after Kriti responded to criticism of her jewellery advertisement, released ahead of Raksha Bandhan. The campaign features the actor in an Indo-Western outfit comprising a bralette-inspired blouse, cape and draped skirt while tying a rakhi.The advertisement also drew criticism from actor-turned-politician Kangana Ranaut, who questioned Kritiâs choice of outfit in the campaign.Addressing the controversy in an Instagram post, Kriti had earlier questioned the practice of judging a woman's respect for culture based on her clothes."The essence of festivals is not in the clothes you wear, it is in the emotions and meaning you hold for the traditions. Rakshabandhan is a bond of protection. My sister and I tie rakhi to each other. We know we can protect each other no less than a brother would have," she said.Sanon said she and her sister pray for each other's "health, happiness & long life", adding that the same wishes extend to their dogs because "they are family!"She also questioned the scrutiny faced by women over their clothing. "Also, when will we stop telling women what to wear??â Sanon said.âEthnic fashion has evolved over the years, but still a woman's respect for her culture is measured with just her clothes!! Culture & Traditions are in her heart, not in her neckline!" she added.Kangana slams Kriti SanonEarlier on Monday, BJP MP Kangana Ranaut also slammed Kriti questioning the styling of the advertisement in an Instagram Story."It's a wonderful time to be a woman. Our closets are full of variety of clothes, today's woman is a global woman," Kangana wrote."From cocktail dresses to lehenga cholis, jeans to saris, bikinis to salwar kameez, from all the options that are available to us today why would you tie your brother a rakhi in your bikini/undergarments? Where are all your styling options? Ha ha the advert looks intentionally creepy!" she added.The advertisement had sparked criticism on social media, with some users questioning whether Sanon's outfit was appropriate for a campaign centred on Raksha Bandhan.One user on X wrote, "Where is Puja Ki thali? Why are you wearing bra in front of your brother? Is this a Raksha Bandhan? Where is Tilak?"Another user criticised the actor, writing, "No woman dresses like this on Raksha Bandhan. Shame on you @kritisanon."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
articles.summary: Iran is no stranger to US sanctions and has developed deep economic ties with several countries.
articles.body:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.

There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.

First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.

Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.

Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.

Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".

It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.

Turkey is another large trading partner of Iran, according to ITC data, but it has a much friendlier relationship with the US than China.

This puts it in a challenging position. The US has threatened to punish those who continue to trade with Iran as part of its economic pressure tactics.

However, economists point out that Turkey cannot stop trading with it without significant damage to its economy, which is already struggling with inflation running at 31.8%, according to official data .

In short, as the only Nato member to share a border with Iran, Turkey has to balance its relationship with military allies and maintaining a relationship with its close economic neighbour.

Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.

But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.

It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.

The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.

The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers , some as young as 15.

This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.

And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.

The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.

Armenia is another major trading partner of Iran, according to the ITC data.

Where it differs the most from others is that its top export partner is Russia, which accounts for 34.9% of all goods sold by Armenia in 2025.

This is despite the fact that Russia has faced sanctions from the US and its allies since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

This suggests Armenia may be willing to continue trading with Iran despite mounting US pressure.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".

Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact.

"So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"

He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".

Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".

She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".

Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.

Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels.

Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.

The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.

Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

articles.title: Air Force officer who died in Alaska plane crash remembered as 'positive leader'
articles.summary: The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah Borsich, 23, as a victim of the deadly Alaska charter plane crash that killed all eight on board near Cape Newenham.
articles.body: A 23-year-old Air Force officer killed alongside seven others in a charter plane crash in remote western Alaska last week is being remembered as a "positive leader" who served with "professionalism, compassion and purpose." The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 450 miles west-southwest of Anchorage. Borsich was a project programmer with the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. "Lt. Borsich was a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command," Col. Timothey Meerstein, commander of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, said in a statement. TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH "She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her," Meerstein said. "She made a lasting impact on our team, and we are grateful for her service and commitment to our nation." The Cessna 441 was carrying two pilots and six passengers when it crashed west of Cape Newenham at about 12:15 p.m. Thursday. All eight people aboard were killed. The charter plane had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and was headed to Cape Newenham when it crashed during its second approach to the gravel runway in heavy fog, according to federal officials. The pilots could not see the runway and were flying by instruments, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said Friday. They aborted their first landing attempt because of poor visibility before crashing on the second approach. An observation system near the airport reported fog and visibility of about 10 miles shortly before the crash. About 15 minutes later, visibility had fallen to less than a quarter-mile, according to the National Weather Service. Search teams later found fragmented wreckage from the twin-engine plane, also known as a Cessna Conquest. The Air Force said an Army member, contractors and crew members with Anchorage-based airplane charter company Security Aviation were also among those killed. "We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten." Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash. "Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy." Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause. "Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said. In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform. Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China. Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said. Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment." "This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the crash. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

"We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten." Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash. "Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy." Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause. "Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said. In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform. Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China. Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said. Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment." "This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash. articles.title: Tyler Robinson's lawyers seek camera ban for Sept. 1 hearing, say case is not a 'reality TV show'
articles.summary: Tyler Robinson's attorneys claim cameras and livestreaming of the Sept. 1 hearing risk turning the Charlie Kirk assassination case into a reality TV show.
articles.body: Tyler Robinson's attorneys are again asking the judge to ban cameras from the courtroom, this time alleging that cameras and streaming of his upcoming Sept. 1 hearing risk turning the case into a "reality TV show." "The media presence in the courtroom both distracts and places added pressure on hearing participants to present for the media, as opposed to focusing on the facts, evidence, and mechanics of the hearing," Robinson's attorneys, Kathy Nester, Michael Burt, Richard Novak and Staci Visser, wrote in one of two Saturday court filings. "Mr. Robinson’s case is not and should not be made into a reality TV show." The defense is arguing that livestreams and other images from the hearing could bias the public against their client by showing evidence that may not be admissible at trial later. TYLER ROBINSON RARELY HIT BULLSEYE IN PRACTICE SHOTS, PUTTING BYSTANDERS AT RISK IN KIRK SHOOTING: PROSECUTORS "Specific to the oral argument on the preliminary hearing, the EMC (electronic media coverage) will memorialize and widely disseminate argument discussing the largely hearsay based evidentiary presentation made by the State," the lawyers wrote. "Such evidence is, by its very nature, insufficiently reliable for admission at trial." Read the filings: Both of the filings also included redacted paragraphs after Robinson's lawyers alleged that, "Additional evidence of bias developing as a result of the widespread publication of this case can be tracked in real time." CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION The defense also claimed that witnesses who provided statements that were admitted as "reliable hearsay" ahead of the week-long July preliminary hearing "experienced harassment by media and interested third parties." Robinson is the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk, 31, at a Turning Point USA event in Orem, Utah, last year. Kirk was shot and killed while speaking to a crowd of thousands at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. JUDGE ALLOWS CAMERAS IN CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION CASE, DELAYS PRELIMINARY HEARING Read the filings: Separately, a source close to the Kirk family said Tuesday that Kirk's widow Erika, and his parents, Rob and Kathy, all plan to attend the Sept. 1 hearing together as they did during the July hearing. CHARLIE KIRK MURDER CASE AS 'STRAIGHT-FORWARD' AS IT GETS, PROSECUTORS ARGUE AS CASE NEARS TRIAL DECISION Judge Tony Graf Jr. will hear oral arguments from both sides regarding the evidence introduced in July and will decide whether there's enough probable cause to justify sending Robinson to trial on the charges against him. GOT A TIP? Robinson's defense objected to hearsay evidence from the preliminary hearing and also opposes the sole aggravating factor in the aggravated murder charge that carries the potential death penalty — that Robinson allegedly put other people at great risk of death by shooting Kirk in a crowded place. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST The defense argued that only a single shot was fired, from an elevated position. It traveled over the crowd, rather than through it, and it only struck Kirk. Prosecutors countered that Robinson was a bad shot, one who "seldom hit the bullseye and sometimes misses the target completely" when practicing shooting with the suspected murder weapon. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Robinson, 23, has not yet entered a plea.

articles.title: SNAP rolls are shrinking fast. This map shows which states have seen the biggest drops.
articles.summary: Nearly 5.6 million fewer people are receiving food assistance than a year ago, with some states seeing much steeper declines.
articles.body:
The number of people receiving food assistance through the nation's largest federal food aid program has fallen by more than 5 million over the past year.

Participation in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has decreased by more than 13% as stricter eligibility rules and work requirements take effect. The biggest declines have been seen in the South and Southwest of the country.

Data released by the USDA this month showed SNAP enrollment provisionally fell to 36.6 million in May 2026 from 42.2 million in May 2025. This provisional figure would make the number of people receiving SNAP as low as it was forecast to reach in 2030, according to the Associated Press.

The decline comes as changes to SNAP have expanded work requirements and tightened eligibility rules as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The changes mean more people must now work, volunteer or take part in job training for at least 80 hours a month to continue receiving SNAP, or risk losing benefits. This rule was extended to include adults up to age 64 and parents of children 14 and older. The law also removed automatic exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youth. Exemptions remain for those 65 and older, parents of children younger than 14, and people with disabilities or health limitations.

Some states have seen sharper drops than others, which you can see in the map below.

In Arizona, the number of people receiving SNAP fell by 53.8% from May 2025 to May 2026, while Georgia saw a 36.5% decline over the same period, according to USDA's figures .

Arizona officials said the drop was driven largely by the state's struggles to put the new federal requirements in place.

"Implementing the federally mandated changes triggered unprecedented call volumes and administrative hurdles, including additional verification requirements, creating real barriers for applicants," Brett Bezio, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Economic Security, told the Associated Press .

Bezio said hiring more staff members and introducing ways for people to submit documents online have helped stem the decline in participation in recent months and reduced the risk that eligible people will lose benefits.

Supporters of the changes introduced by the OBBBA argue that tighter eligibility rules will reduce improper payments and encourage more adults to work.

In an article looking into the fall in SNAP participants last week, the Cato Institute said: "Much of SNAP's enrollment decline reflects states unwinding pandemic-era waivers and eligibility rules that kept caseloads elevated."

It added, "Judge the success of OBBBA's SNAP reforms, and all welfare programs, by how many people move out of welfare and into self-sufficiency, not by how many are kept on it."

Grocery prices in U.S. cities have risen 33% since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures. By comparison, they rose just 6.4% over the previous seven-and-a-half years.

In Florida, where SNAP participation fell 22% in the year to May 2026, Paco Velez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said part of the decline may be driven by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown if they seek government benefits.

Critics of the SNAP reforms say the new requirements create administrative hurdles that can cause eligible people to lose food assistance.

Some food banks have increased food distributions to try to meet demand that they say has risen as SNAP participation has declined. But advocates say they cannot fully make up the difference.

Reflecting on the changes to SNAP earlier this month, nonprofit No Kid Hungry said: "Already 4.5 million people, including over a million kids, have lost access to SNAP over the past year. Those families are now missing out on the nutritious food SNAP provides, and sadly that number will only grow."

The decline may not be over. Starting in October 2027, states will have to pay a share of SNAP benefit costs if their payment error rates exceed 6% — a change advocates warn could push states to tighten eligibility further to avoid the added expense, potentially creating new barriers for recipients in the years ahead.

articles.title: Mentmore Towers, Batman Beginsâ Wayne Manor in Buckinghamshire, could be seized as owners face deadline to repair crumbling mansion and conduct bat surveys to save historic property
articles.summary: UK News: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after .
articles.body: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after the Grade I-listed mansion was served with a formal repairs notice. The property could ultimately face a compulsory purchase order if its owners fail to take action, while authorities have also required specialist bat surveys before restoration work can proceed.Mentmore Towers, the sprawling country house that doubled as Bruce Wayneâs iconic home in Batman Begins, has been described as being in âvery badâ condition by Historic England. Buckinghamshire Council has now issued a listed-building repairs notice, saying the work is âreasonably necessary for the proper preservationâ of the historic property.The notice comes amid concerns over the deterioration of the mansion, including its roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. Photographs included in the notice reportedly show cracks in walls, broken windows and ivy-covered walls. During a visit to the property, officials also found evidence of bats, according to SWNS.Batmanâs Wayne Manor faces a preservation battleMentmore Towers was built between 1852 and 1854 for the Rothschild family and is considered the only major surviving work of architect Sir Joseph Paxton, who also designed Londonâs Crystal Palace.The mansion later gained global pop-culture recognition when it was used as Wayne Manor in Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins. The property has also appeared in films including The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English.Its cinematic history, however, has not prevented growing concerns about its physical condition.Buckinghamshire Council has ordered the owners to demonstrate that they are appointing a contractor with experience in repairing listed buildings. The authorities have also required three bat-emergence surveys to be completed by August 2027, along with any necessary Natural England licence and recommendations arising from the surveys.Once repair work begins, council and Historic England officers must also be permitted to inspect the property weekly.Council warns of possible compulsory purchaseThe repairs notice represents a significant escalation in the long-running concerns surrounding Mentmore Towers.If the required action is not taken, Buckinghamshire Council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion through a compulsory purchase order, alongside pursuing further legal action.The development has been welcomed by heritage campaigners.Henrietta Billings, director of SAVE Britainâs Heritage, said the organisation welcomed Buckinghamshire Councilâs decision to require the current owner to undertake âurgent and overdue repairsâ to the historic house.âWe urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs,â she said. âThis exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long.âWho owns the real Wayne Manor?Mentmore Towers is owned by Syrian-British businessman Simon Halabi, who purchased the property in 1999 after it had been put up for sale two years earlier.Halabi had ambitious plans for the estate, intending to transform Mentmore Towers into a luxury hotel featuring 171 suites.Those plans became embroiled in a legal battle in 2004 after local resident Jonathan Davey obtained a last-minute injunction at the High Court to stop the proposed development.A judicial review subsequently examined whether the conditions attached to the planning permission had been followed. In March 2005, the High Court ruled that the decision to grant planning permission was âunimpeachableâ.However, the proposed luxury hotel never became a reality. Halabiâs property company later ran into financial difficulties amid the collapse of the housing market, and the hotel plans were abandoned.From Rothschild mansion to Batmanâs Wayne ManorBefore Halabi acquired the property, Mentmore Towers had already undergone several changes in its history.In 1992, the previous owners established a country club at the estate, complete with an 18-hole golf course. The club eventually ceased trading in 2015.More recently, company documents filed with Companies House in May reportedly show that Mentmore Towers Ltd, of which Halabi is a director, is a dormant company, meaning it is not currently trading or generating other income such as investments.Despite the uncertainty surrounding its future, Mentmore Towers remains one of Britainâs most recognisable historic estates.Mentmore Towersâ Hollywood historyFor Batman fans, the property is best known as Wayne Manor in Batman Begins, where it provided the exterior setting for Bruce Wayneâs ancestral home.But its screen history extends well beyond Gotham.Mentmore Towers has featured in The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English, while its grand interiors and distinctive architecture have also appeared in music videos.The mansion was used in Haddawayâs âWhat Is Loveâ music video and the Spice Girlsâ âGoodbyeâ video.Now, however, the historic building faces a very real battle far removed from the fictional world of Batman. Unless the necessary repairs, ecological surveys and preservation measures are carried out, the future of the real-life Wayne Manor could ultimately be decided by the authorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Who was aboard mystery US aircraft that landed in Russia? Report reveals
articles.summary: Europe News: A US Air Force C-17 military transport aircraft landed at Moscowâs Vnukovo Airport on Tuesday, triggering speculation over who was aboard and why the .
articles.body: A US Air Force C-17 military transport aircraft landed at Moscowâs Vnukovo Airport on Tuesday, triggering speculation over who was aboard and why the aircraft had flown to Russia at a time when US-Russia contacts over the Ukraine war have slowed.According to Axios, CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow on Tuesday for meetings with Russian officials, citing two US officials. The report said Ratcliffe departed Washington on Sunday, travelled to Latvia aboard a US government aircraft and then flew from Riga to Moscow on a US Air Force C-17.CBS News also reported that Ratcliffe was in Moscow for meetings, citing sources familiar with the situation. If confirmed, it would mark Ratcliffeâs first known trip to Russia since becoming CIA director and the highest-level visit by a Trump administration official to the country since January.The reports came after a Boeing C-17A Globemaster III was spotted at Vnukovo alongside a US diplomatic motorcade. articles.title: Florida voters have approved $35 million to buy and transform 5.8 miles of underused railroad into a trail that will form part of an 11.4-mile greenway and help close a gap in a planned 400-mile trail network
articles.summary: US News: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to.
articles.body: Voters in the coastal Florida city of Bonita Springs have approved a $35 million general obligation bond, clearing the way for the local government to buy a key 5.8-mile stretch of unused railway. The ballot decision unlocks the missing central section of the wider 11.4-mile Bonita Estero Rail Trail (BERT). The project will also help close an important gap in the planned Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a 400-mile network that is intended to run across Southwest Florida. The referendum was held during the 18 August primary election. It allows the city council to issue up to $35 million in general obligation bonds with a 30-year repayment period. According to public election filings, $28.6 million will be used to buy the 5.8-mile inactive railway corridor from the Fay family, owners of the Seminole Gulf Railway. The rest will pay for engineering, design and the first stage of construction from downtown Bonita Springs.Completing the regional puzzleThe vote removes the final financial hurdle to buying the full 11.4-mile railway corridor, which covers about 180 acres across Southwest Florida. Neighbouring authorities had already committed money to secure their parts of the line. The Village of Estero to the north pledged $19.8 million to buy nearly four miles of track, while Collier County to the south committed $11.6 million for its 1.5-mile section. The combined purchase price agreed by the three jurisdictions is $60 million, about 20 per cent below the property's total appraised value. Because Bonita Springs lies between Estero and Collier County, its approval was seen by conservation groups as the key step needed to secure the entire corridor. "With the positive vote from Bonita Spring residents, we have the final piece in place for the purchase of the rail corridor for BERT," said Deb Orton, President of Friends of BERT, in a statement released through the Trust for Public Land. "Our next step is to complete the due diligence efforts that move us closer to the finalization of the purchase in October. The voters have given the Bonita Springs City Council a clear mandate they sought when they voted to place the referendum on the August 18th ballot for consideration."Cost and local debateThe $35 million bond will be repaid through local property taxes over 30 years. Financial estimates from PFM Financial Advisors show that the measure will add between $49 and $88 a year to the property tax bill for an average home valued at $441,137. Supporters, including the Naples Pathway Coalition, said this works out to about $4.75 a month per household. The project received strong support from local businesses and conservation groups, but there was also opposition before the vote. Some homeowners living next to the unused tracks raised concerns about privacy and security because of increased public access. Others questioned the cost of the project or suggested keeping the corridor available for possible light rail in the future. City leaders, however, argued that turning the abandoned railway into a paved path for walkers and cyclists would provide greater public benefits. They pointed to improved pedestrian safety, better regional connections and potential benefits for local businesses.A wider conservation projectThe Trust for Public Land (TPL), a national non-profit focused on land conservation and public parks, has played a major role in the project. TPL worked with city officials, the Naples Pathway Coalition and Friends of BERT volunteers on the corridor's valuation and public campaign. "Today, Bonita Springs voters made a bold endorsement to invest in a better future for their community," said Doug Hattaway, Southeast Region Conservation Director at Trust for Public Land. "Voters have resoundingly authorized its City Council to fund the corridor's purchase along with significant construction funding of the 5.8-mile Bonita Springs portion of the longer 11.4-mile rails-to-trails project involving also the Village of Estero to the north and Collier County to the south." The completed 11.4-mile trail will give runners, walkers and cyclists a new regional route while also connecting with the planned 75-mile Paradise Coast Trail, which is expected to stretch from Marco Island to South Lee County. The Paradise Coast Trail will then connect with the larger Florida Gulf Coast Trail, a planned 400-mile route linking communities from Naples towards the Tampa Bay area. With voters now approving the bond, city officials and project partners are conducting environmental checks and completing property assessments before the purchase is formally closed. The transaction is expected to be completed in October. Design work for the first paved sections in central Bonita Springs is expected to begin soon after the purchase is finalised.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 200,000 visas could be revoked by the Trump administration. Here's who's affected and what happens next
articles.summary: The State Department is expected to announce the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued over the past decade.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is preparing to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourist visas held by foreign nationals who have applied for or are seeking asylum in the U.S., according to department documents obtained by the Associated Press .

The State Department is reportedly going to announce the action in the coming weeks. If the plans are carried out, it is believed it would represent the largest single mass visa revocation in U.S. history.

"We are coordinating with Department of Homeland Security to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the Associated Press .

Here's what you need to know about what visas the government is targeting and what happens next.

The State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of B-1 and B-2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum.

Foreign nationals apply for a temporary B-1 visa or B-2 visa if they are visiting the U.S. for business or tourism.

Foreign nationals entering the country for business apply for B-1 visas to attend a business convention or conference, settle an estate, negotiate a contract or meet with business associates.

B-2 visas are for people visiting the U.S. on vacation. They would also apply for those seeing friends or relatives, seeking medical treatment, competing in amateur competitions or taking recreational courses that are not university-accredited.

Visa holders are usually let into the country for six months at a time. Border officers have some flexibility to admit someone for longer, up to a year, and if that's still not enough, people can apply to USCIS for a further extension, usually another six months.

Holding a B-1 or B-2 visa doesn't stop someone from applying for asylum. The two are entirely separate immigration processes, and doing one doesn't require or exclude the other.

However, when current applicants apply for a B-1 or B-2 visa, they are asked to confirm that they intend to return to their home country and are not planning to seek asylum, according to AP.

Under federal law , both immigrant and nonimmigrant visas can be revoked by the State Department at any time, including after someone has already traveled to the U.S.

Courts generally can't second-guess that decision, either. There's almost no way to challenge a visa revocation in court. The only exception is if someone is already in deportation proceedings and the revoked visa is the sole reason they're being removed, according to a Congressional Research Service report published in July.

If someone's B-1 or B-2 visa is revoked and they are already living in the U.S., if they leave the country for any reason, even briefly, they likely won't be allowed to re-enter. Their old visa would be void, so they'd have to apply for a new one from abroad, with no guarantee it would be approved.

Canceling someone's visa does not mean they will be immediately deported. Revoking a visa and deporting someone are two separate legal actions, handled by two different government agencies. The State Department can cancel a visa, but it takes a separate decision by the Department of Homeland Security to actually start the deportation process. Until that happens, the person isn't removed.

Someone whose visa is revoked doesn't lose every legal protection. If they're placed in deportation proceedings, they're still entitled to a hearing. That said, unlike in criminal cases, the government won't provide them a lawyer; they'd need to find one themselves or seek free legal aid.

People with pending claims could be recategorized but lose their status as business or tourism travelers, according to the AP report.

The State Department is expected to formally announce the plan in the coming weeks, though nothing is final yet. No policy has been published in the Federal Register, and officials have cautioned that both the scope and the process could still change before it's carried out.

Pigott, the State Department spokesperson, has said the process would be rolling rather than a single announcement: "As the process will be ongoing, the number of revocations remains dynamic and will be done on a rolling basis."

Legal challenges are widely expected. Courts have already pushed back on a related immigration move by the administration: a federal judge recently vacated Secretary of State Marco Rubio's suspension of immigrant visa processing from 75 countries, ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.

The Trump administration has so far revoked about 175,000 visas , the State Department said in August, the majority of which were due to "law enforcement encounters" such as assault, driving under the influence, theft, and drug crimes. Overstays and public criticism of U.S. policy have also been cited as reasons .

A brief timeline of immigration actions since January 2025

Jan. 20, 2025: Trump returns to office and signs an executive order seeking to limit birthright citizenship , launching a broad immigration crackdown.

May 27, 2025: The State Department pauses new student visa interview appointments worldwide for F, M and J visas, as it moves to expand social media vetting.

June 4, 2025: A presidential proclamation bars full or partial entry to the U.S. from 19 countries.

Jan. 12, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative visa revocation total has surpassed 100,000 since Trump's inauguration, including about 8,000 student visas.

Jan. 14-21, 2026: The State Department announces a "full review" of screening policies , then pauses immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries.

Feb. 2, 2026: Plaintiffs sue Secretary of State Rubio over the 75-country visa pause.

June 30, 2026: The Supreme Court affirms birthright citizenship, striking down the president's Jan. 2025 order.

Aug. 6, 2026: Trump signs two executive orders in a new attempt to curtail birthright citizenship, despite June's Supreme Court ruling rejecting his previous effort.

Aug. 10, 2026: The State Department discloses the cumulative total of visas revoked has reached more than 175,000 since Trump's inauguration. This is at a pace of more than 10,000 revocations a month in 2026, up from about 8,000 a month in 2025.

Aug. 21, 2026: A federal judge vacates Rubio's 75-country visa pause , ruling it exceeded his statutory authority.
